PRIDE

By: Hein Kaiser | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
we have one of the most progressive constitutions in the world but, on the ground, it doesn't taste like freedom for the LGBTQ community

Unique Selling Point:
It's a story about being human and holds universal themes that we can all identify with. The struggle of the underdog who makes it. And at the same time we tell the story of the LBGTQ community and creating a sense of seeking for justice, another universal and easily identifiable theme for all of us. And it is very relevant in South African society, right now.

Summary:
It's been 32 years since the first Pride event in Johannesburg. Since then, our Constitution guaranteed the rights of the LBGTQ community to be equal to those of others. Yet, in reality, on the ground, life looks very different with discrimination, hate crimes and prejudice. And yet, the LGBTQ community continues to overcome these obstacles, too, in pursuit of equality.

Further information:
The insert is a metaphor for all of humanity. It's a narrative of self-realisation against all odds, too. The LGTBQ community is a vehicle, or character, that we can all look at and take lessons from.

We meet Mike, who has lived through pre-constitution days and said that until today, nothing has changed bar the constitution. He is the CEO of a large medical group, where he is majority shareholder, and a company he started when he quit his job at a casino group to escape prejudice and being called a moffie. Recently, his partner passed away, and Mike is at odds with a family that could still not accept that their son was gay. They even slept in separate rooms in a facade made to measure for his partner's family.

Clive Vanderwagen realised he was gay while in service of the Methodist Church. He was pretty much excommunicated when he came out, and stripped of all his responsibilities in the church. He was so desperate to be straight ad claim back his life, that he underwent conversion therapy. For 12 years he lived a lie until he could no more.

Nomfundo Ndaba is the CEO of FEW, a rights organisation that focuses on Gay and Lesbian rights. FEW are also the organisers of the Soweto Pride event, which she said, is the one day that people who normally live in hiding can come out, stamp their feet and be themselves. She tells of the tragic hate crimes that the LBGTQ community endures frequently and, her emotional story of coming out after being married to a man, first, to hide who she really is. She turned the prejudice she felt into energy to fight the good fight for everyone who feels still alone.

Inbetween, vox pops will tell a narrative of the many people and permutations in the LBGTQ community as well as some of the elements of prejudice that people feel, inside the community.

SCRIPT
VO:

To be or not to be at all. It’s still a question.

For decades the LGBTQ+ community were not allowed to be. If you were different to the norm, you were… other. And that could have landed you in hot water.

When you dared to fall in love in the past, you could be locked up.

Upsound: FUNDI
One day you realize that you are black. Once you realise that you are LGBTI, we may next to realize that that the world is not as kind as it should be
VO:

Being different was illegal until our constitution set South Africa on a new course of inclusion after 1994.

It’s been three decades of freedom to choose, but in those thirty years we have not seemed to move at the same speed as the law.

The recent Pride parades celebrate this freedom, but it also reminds us of the long road of real acceptance we still need to travel.

VOXIE
Pride parade is a form of protest. It may seem that it's become a party, but it is still a protest, and it does spark a new conversation.
Upsound: Clive Vanderwagen

I was terrified that I was going to be discovered. I was terrified that it was going to affect my career.
VO
Being able to shed the burden of being different can have a beautiful outcome.
Wellness media personality Dr Dulcy Rakumakoe is living her dream to take quality healthcare to disadvantaged South Africans. Her Sandton office is a hive of activity and her schedule punishing.
VO
Yet Dr Dulcy will pause everything to share the fairy-tale that life has afforded her and her wife Vanessa.
DULCY
I saw a picture on Facebook. A Beautiful woman wearing a yellow dress, So I saved the picture on my phone and started telling my friends that this is the woman I'm going to marry

VO
And the couple eventually tied the knot, but it was not without possible headwinds like culture and tradition.
DULCY
We were asking her to leave her culture now to become one with us.
MASA
In that case, who pays lobola?
DULCY
I paid lobola because I was going to her parents to ask for her hand in marriage,
VO
First, the couple had a traditional wedding and a few months later, the glowing brides tied the knot at a breath-taking white wedding.
It was a love story that ended in a dream wedding.
But even though it’s possible to get married today, not every part of it brims with romance. The paperwork still has a sting in the tail.
DULCY
When we went to Home Affairs, their paperwork was still very male female, you still had to read I the husband and my partner being the wife, you know, meaning like so many years later, we still have not really done the work, you know, in making sure that all the institutions are sensitized and safe for our people.
LINK
What's it like to feel different? To be, but not to be. The LGBTQ community has grappled with what it means to be OK for decades, and it still seems that there's a sense of being other.
VOX POP
We are still unaccepting of people, of different cultures, races, languages, even, and just lifestyles in general.
VOX POP
Back then it was just gay, lesbian, bisexual, maybe three things. And now it's turned into a whole dictionary.
VO
And while the acronym is evolving, at the moment it stands for lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, intersex, queer/questioning and asexual. There are many other terms, too, that people use to describe their personal versions and experiences of their gender, sexuality and biological sex aspects.
VO
Clive Vanderwagen is an internal dynamics facilitator for companies, he’s a successful writer and speaker who’s shared some of his experiences on various platforms including the global platform, Ted Talks.
But before Clive turned adversity into personal victory, he struggled with the reality of who he was. And it was particularly difficult for him because of his choice of career.
He wanted to become a minister
CLIVE
I had known I was gay since I was a child. And I had been hiding this.
VO
If he was discovered, Clive stood to lose everything. After three years of being employed as a youth minister the church had provided a roof over his head and he was at the beginnings of a career in service of the cloth.
There was no place in the ministry for a gay man at the time.

CLIVE
If the people that I had told kind of came out and said something that I would be fired, I would lose my home and my family would be shunned because they were part of the church. It was terrifying.

CLIVE
So, the process was, is that if I could somehow become straight, I it would be fine.
VO
The church believed that Clive could be cured from his homosexuality and that offered some hope for a man trapped between who he knew he was and the damage it could do to his chosen journey.
Clyde wanted to rid himself of the burden of being gay.
Conversion therapy promised to do just that.
MASA
You were chasing a cure and that's how you were able to remain in the church as long as you're willing to fix yourself.
CLIVE
The way conversion therapy works is, you claim your heterosexuality, so you walk in freedom. I kept asking why I don't feel attracted to women and they said because God doesn't replace one lust with another. So, what I needed to do was get into a relationship with a woman and I needed to walk in victory.
VO
He could call himself ex-gay after being “converted” … And while eventually he fell in love with a woman emotionally, he was not attracted to her.
reality hit home….and it hit him hard when it did.
CLIVE
I was at a conference, an ex-gay conference, and one of the people who at the same church as I arrived at the conference, I knew he was gay, but he was married with kids. but he was having affairs on the side, and he was now HIV positive and infected his wife.
VO
The conversion therapy did not work for Clive either, but the wages of his own truth was to lose everything.

CLIVE
I went to the church, and I said to them that I don't think I'm as healed as I thought I was.
MASA
What was their reaction to that?
CLIVE
They removed me from all aspects of ministry. and I was unclean.
MASA
So, what did that feel like being stripped away from these people who are essentially your family?
CLIVE
It was difficult because it was really my identity was found in the church. I felt stripped of my identity. I had my recognition and value in terms of my purpose in life was around the church and ministering to other people. So, when they removed me from that, I kind of had to reconcile who I was. What did I how could I have purpose? And when I felt called to be in ministry by God, yet God refused to heal me. And I couldn't reconcile the two.
VOXIE:
My son came and approached me and spoke to me and said, Dad, I'm gay. I would support it wholeheartedly. Would it be a difficult pill to swallow? And I would have to answer that yes as well. I don't think it's because of his decision or not accepting his decision. It's purely because of the fact that in our society, in South Africa, it isn't a decision that is accepted wholeheartedly. And I know it would be a difficult journey for him to travel,
VOX POP
we are born the way we are we can't change it and we shouldn't be treated any different from any other human being.
Upsound FUNDI
When people know that you're gay. Homophobic. People would want to direct the phobias and challenges and violence against you.
VO
Nomfundo Ndaba from the Women’s Empowerment Forum said that there have been 34 recorded hate crimes against the LGBTQ+ community since 2020.
It seems we’re somewhat behind the curve.
FUNDI
I think South Africa created a faulty approach in having this constitution that they were not able to translate into tangible meaning., the police, the nurses, the health system, the school and all didn't create an inclusive approach.
DULCY
when you when you are advocating for queer rights, like people tend to act or understand you as if you are looking for special rights for special people, you know. But you are just wanting the Constitution as it is applied in South Africa that is safe for everyone. The queer people deserve it, too.
CLIVE
But on the ground, there is still a need for more visibility. There is still a need for and especially within certain communities, we are seeing lesbian women in many pockets of South African society being murdered for being lesbian women. It's there is still a sense of being other. There is still discrimination, there is still a sense of you don't fit the standard
The biggest change, I suppose, is how I have dealt with my sexuality and the fact that I don't really care anymore.
VO
Clive decided to be who he is. So did everyone that shared their stories with us.
And this could also be a metaphor for all of us to consider. Because when someone is different to us, that’s all it is. Different.
EXTENDED VOXIE
If you look at issues like racism, for example, it's still an issue in this country. And as much as we've made headway in that, and it's been it's been years; it's been it's been decades and decades that people have been fighting against it
It's still going to happen until people reach a point where they are more accepting. And that's going to take time to change.
